content: Hypertrophy requires 10-20 sets per muscle group per week. Overload via weight, volume, or frequency. Beyond 20 sets/week yields diminishing returns.
Distribute weekly volume across 2-3 sessions per muscle group. Higher frequency allows greater total weekly volume than once-weekly training.
Strength (1-5 reps): rest 3-5 min. Hypertrophy compounds: 2-3 min. Isolation: 1-2 min. Longer rest allows more volume.
Hypertrophy occurs across 6-30 reps if taken near failure. 1-5 reps optimal for strength. 8-12 reps balance tension and metabolic stress.
Structure 4-8 week mesocycles. Final week: deload with 40-50% volume reduction and/or 10-20% intensity reduction.
Program 60-80% compound exercises, 20-40% isolation. Compounds allow heavier loads and recruit more muscle mass.
Maintain 1:1 push-to-pull ratio or favor pulling. Include unilateral work. Address asymmetries >10-15%.
Beginners (0-12 months): 3-4 days/week, full-body or upper/lower. Linear progression. 3-5 sets per exercise. Focus technique.
Advanced lifters (3+ years): may need 15-25+ sets/muscle/week. Use drop sets, rest-pause, cluster sets on 1-2 exercises/session.
Adults 40+: prioritize technique over load. Use 8-15 reps. Allow longer recovery. Include balance work.
Women respond similarly to men in relative gains. Use all rep ranges including 1-5 reps. Balance upper/lower body work.
Include all patterns: squat, hinge, horizontal push/pull, vertical push/pull, single-leg. Keep core lifts 4-8 weeks, rotate accessories.
Program 60-70% bilateral (primary strength), 30-40% unilateral (address asymmetries, core stability, reduce spinal load).
Core training: emphasize anti-extension (planks), anti-lateral flexion (side planks), anti-rotation (Pallof press). 2-3x/week.
Power: 30-60% 1RM for max power output. Perform early in session when fresh. Full recovery 3-5 min between sets.
Grip: timed holds at 80-100% deadlift max for 10-30s. Farmer walks. Fat grips. Grip strength correlates with longevity.
Train within 0-3 reps of failure for hypertrophy. Compounds: stop 1-3 RIR. Isolation: 0-1 RIR is well-tolerated.
Agonist-antagonist supersets (chest/back, biceps/triceps) cut training time 50% with similar hypertrophy. Rest 2-3 min between pairs.
Cluster sets: 10-20s intra-set rest between rep clusters. Maintains bar velocity. Best for power and heavy strength work.
Drop sets: train to failure, reduce 20-30%, repeat. Use on isolation/machines. 1-2 exercises/session max. Reduces training time 40-50%.
Taper for competition: reduce volume 40-60%, maintain intensity. 1-2 weeks optimal. Peak performance within first 2 weeks of reduced training.
VBT zones: <0.30 m/s max strength (>85% 1RM), 0.45-0.75 m/s strength-speed, 0.75-1.0 m/s speed-strength, >1.0 m/s power (<55% 1RM).
Youth training: emphasize technique with light loads. Avoid failure. 1-2 sets, 8-15 reps. 2-3 sessions/week. Qualified supervision required.
Muscle protein synthesis elevated 24-48h post-training. Train each muscle 2-3x/week for repeated MPS spikes.
RPE 8 = 2 RIR. RPE 9 = 1 RIR. RPE 10 = failure. Hypertrophy: most sets RPE 7-9. Strength: RPE 7-9.5. Power: RPE 6-7.5.
Controlled eccentric 2-4 seconds maximizes time under tension. Eccentric training creates more muscle damage—allow extra recovery.
Full ROM generally superior for muscle development. Partial ROM for: working around injuries, overloading specific positions.
Terminate set if form breaks down. Neutral spine, controlled tempo, joints aligned. Ego lifting is primary injury cause.
Wide tempo range (2-8s/rep) produces similar hypertrophy if near failure. Very slow (>10s/rep) requires too-light loads.
Lengthened partials (bottom ROM) may equal or exceed full ROM for hypertrophy. Shortened partials for lockout strength only.
Isometrics build strength specific to trained angle (±15°). Use multiple angles for full ROM strength. 3-6s holds for strength.
Valsalva for heavy lifts: deep breath, brace core, hold through rep, exhale after. Increases force production 5-15%.
Static stretching pre-training reduces force 5-10%. Use dynamic stretching in warm-up. Static stretching post-training or separate sessions.
Warm-up: 5-10 min aerobic, dynamic stretching, specific warm-up sets with progressive loading. Needs increase with age and load.
Overtraining signs: declining performance despite training, persistent soreness, elevated resting HR 5-10 bpm above baseline. Implement deloads.
Training around injury: avoid aggravating movements, train uninjured parts, reduce load while maintaining movement patterns. Pain that worsens = stop.
Static stretching 30-60s per muscle, 2-3x/week for flexibility gains. Hip, ankle, thoracic, shoulder mobility critical for compound lifts.
Separate cardio and strength by 6-8 hours to minimize interference. Low-intensity cardio produces minimal interference with strength gains.
HIIT: 30s-4 min high intensity, equal or longer recovery, 15-30 min total. Limit to 2-3 sessions/week if prioritizing strength.
LISS (50-70% max HR, 30-60 min) builds aerobic base with minimal interference. Can be performed daily without compromising strength recovery.
Internal focus increases muscle activation 10-15% on isolation exercises. Use external cues for compound movements.
High-bar: upright torso, more quad. Low-bar: forward lean, more posterior chain. Full depth (hip below knee) superior for development.
Velocity loss in set: 10-20% for strength with low fatigue. 20-40% for hypertrophy. >40% creates excessive fatigue without added benefit.
External cues ('push the bar away') outperform internal cues ('contract your chest') for compound movements. Action verbs enhance force.
Deadlift: bar over midfoot, neutral spine, shoulders over bar. Initiate with leg drive, not back extension. Longer torso may favor sumo.
Bench: scapulae retracted and depressed. Elbow 45-70° from torso. Touch between nipples and sternum. Narrower grip reduces shoulder stress.
Longer limbs create leverage disadvantages on most lifts. Select exercises accounting for individual anatomy. Bands/chains match natural strength curves.
Rows: initiate with scapular retraction, then elbow flexion. Horizontal rows for thickness, vertical pulls for width. Control eccentric.
1RM protocol: warm-up to 60-80%, then 85-95%, then attempts. 3-5 min rest between attempts. Most reach true 1RM in 3-5 attempts.
HRV 20%+ below baseline suggests incomplete recovery—reduce intensity/volume. Track 7-day rolling average, not daily fluctuations.
Use same method, same conditions, track trends. DEXA 1-3% error. BIA 3-8% error. Progress photos + measurements often sufficient.
VBT implementation: test load-velocity profile, prescribe by velocity zone, adjust daily load to hit target velocity. Objective autoregulation.
Test baseline before program, check every 4-8 weeks, post-program assessment. Standardize conditions. Over-testing creates fatigue.
Experienced lifters estimate RIR within 1-2 reps. Beginners need 6-12 weeks practice. Combine RPE with objective metrics for best monitoring.
Free weights: greater stabilizer activation, steeper learning curve. Machines: safer failure, muscle isolation. 60-75% free weights, 20-30% machines.
Bands: accommodating resistance, low joint stress, portable. Similar hypertrophy to weights when volume and effort matched. Best as supplement.
Protein: 1.6-2.2 g/kg/day. 0.25-0.40 g/kg per meal (20-40g). Distribute every 3-4 hours. 2-3g leucine per meal maximizes MPS.
Carbs: 3-5 g/kg/day for strength training. 6-10 g/kg/day for high volume/endurance. Post-workout 0.8-1.2 g/kg within 30-60 min for glycogen.
Fats: minimum 20-35% calories, 0.5-1 g/kg. Below 15% calories can suppress testosterone 10-15%. Balance omega-6:omega-3 ratio 4:1 or lower.
Total daily intake > precise timing. Protein within 3-4 hours post-workout supports recovery. 3-6 protein-containing meals per day.
Muscle gain: 200-500 calorie surplus (10-20%). Target 0.5-1.0% bodyweight gain/month. Larger surplus = excessive fat gain.
Fat loss: 300-500 calorie deficit (15-25%). 0.5-1.0% bodyweight loss/week. Increase protein to 2.0-2.4 g/kg. Maintain training intensity.
Creatine monohydrate: 3-5g daily. 5-15% strength increase, 1-2kg lean mass gain. Safe, no loading required. Most effective supplement.
Caffeine: 3-6 mg/kg, 30-60 min pre-workout. 3-7% power increase. Avoid within 6 hours of bedtime. Cycle use to prevent tolerance.
Beta-alanine: 3-6g daily split into 1.5-2g doses. Benefits activities 1-4 min duration. Takes 2-4 weeks to increase carnosine.
Common athlete deficiencies: iron, magnesium, zinc, vitamin D, B vitamins. Food first; targeted supplementation based on blood testing.
IF can work for fat loss but no metabolic advantage. May impair muscle gain if limiting protein. Protein distribution 3-5 hours generally superior.
Ketogenic diets impair high-intensity performance. Suboptimal for strength and muscle gain. Not recommended for maximizing athletic performance.
Plant-based: 1.8-2.4 g/kg protein. Combine sources for complete amino acids. Supplement B12, consider creatine, iron with vitamin C.
Collagen: 15-20g with 50-100mg vitamin C, 30-60 min before tendon-loading exercise. May enhance tendon repair and injury prevention.
Post-activation potentiation: heavy lift (85-95% 1RM, 3-5 reps) then explosive movement after 3-8 min. Works best in trained individuals.
Blood flow restriction: 20-40% 1RM, 3-4 sets of 15-30 reps, 30-45s rest. 40-80% occlusion pressure. Use for rehab or volume without joint stress.
Type II dominant: respond to lower reps (1-8), higher intensity. Type I dominant: tolerate higher reps (12-20+), higher volume. Train varied ranges.
Tendon adapts slower than muscle (12-24 weeks vs 8-12 weeks). High-magnitude loading >70% MVC. 48-72h recovery between loading sessions.
Bone density: requires >70% 1RM loads, multi-directional loading, impact activities. Site-specific adaptation. 1-3% spine BMD increase over 12-24 months.
Follicular phase (days 1-14): generally favorable for high-intensity training. Luteal phase (days 15-28): may need 50-100 more calories, more carbs.
ACSM strength loading: novice 8-12RM, intermediate/advanced 1-6RM periodized. Power: 0-60% 1RM lower body, 30-60% 1RM upper body.
Muscular endurance: 40-60% 1RM for >15 reps with short rest (<90s). Light loads, high reps, minimal rest.
ACSM training frequency: novice 2-3 days/week, intermediate 3-4 days/week, advanced 4-5 days/week.
Load progression: increase 2-10% when athlete can complete 1-2 reps over target. Smaller increments for upper body, larger for lower.
Optimal hypertrophy: 12-20 sets/muscle/week for trained individuals. >20 sets shows minimal additional gains for most muscles except triceps.
Volume thresholds: <12 sets/week = low, 12-20 sets/week = moderate (optimal), >20 sets/week = high (diminishing returns for most muscles).
Novice: full-body 3x/week. Intermediate: upper/lower 4x/week. Advanced: PPL or body part splits 5-6x/week. Match frequency to volume needs.
Exercise order: compound before isolation, multi-joint before single-joint, weaker areas first when fresh. Power exercises always first.
Warm-up sets: 40-50% x 8-10, 60-70% x 5-6, 80-85% x 2-3, then working sets. More sets needed for heavier loads.
Prioritize weak points early in session when fresh. Accessory work 2-4 sets per exercise. Rotate accessories every 4-6 weeks.
Session structure: 45-75 min optimal. 4-6 exercises typical. Main lift + 2-3 accessories + core. Longer sessions = diminishing focus and recovery.
Deload every 4-8 weeks depending on intensity. Reduce volume 40-60%, maintain intensity. Alternatively: reduce intensity 10-20%, maintain volume.
Per-session volume cap: 6-10 sets per muscle group max. Beyond 10 sets/muscle/session shows diminished returns. Split volume across days.
Strength progression: beginners add load weekly, intermediates every 2-4 weeks, advanced monthly or longer. Slower progression = longer career.
